nameStory: The 'oneseed bur cucumber' gets its name from its spiky, bur-like fruits that contain just a single seed each - quite different from regular cucumbers with their many seeds! The 'star-cucumber' nickname comes from the way its palmately lobed leaves spread out like points of a star. Despite the cucumber connection, you definitely wouldn't want this wild relative on your salad plate.
description: Oneseed bur cucumber is a fast-growing annual vine that scrambles over other plants or forms dense mats on the ground. This member of the gourd family uses curly tendrils to grab onto whatever it can climb, often covering fences, shrubs, and garden plants by late summer. The vine produces small, inconspicuous greenish flowers and distinctive clusters of tiny, spiky fruits that look like miniature medieval maces. It's a native plant that can quickly cover large areas during the growing season.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Clusters of very small, spiky bur-like fruits about the size of large peas, each containing just one seed. The fruits feel prickly to touch and stick to clothing and fur like tiny velcro balls.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Palm-shaped leaves with 3-5 pointed lobes radiating from the center like a maple leaf, but thinner and more delicate. The leaves feel slightly rough and papery to touch.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing vine that uses thin, curly tendrils to grab onto other plants, or spreads as a mat over the ground. Can quickly cover large areas in a single growing season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous green to yellowish-green flowers in small clusters. Male and female flowers are separate but on the same plant, and you need to look closely to even notice them.

habitat: Look for oneseed bur cucumber in moist, rich soils along stream banks, pond edges, and in floodplains throughout New England. It thrives in disturbed areas like garden edges, fence rows, and anywhere the soil stays reasonably moist during summer. You'll often find it scrambling over other vegetation in partially shaded to sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, with first leaves appearing as small, star-shaped seedlings in rich, moist soil.
seasonality.summer: Rapid vine growth and climbing occurs, with tiny greenish flowers blooming throughout mid to late summer. The plant quickly covers available space during peak growing season.
seasonality.fall: Distinctive spiky bur fruits ripen and become most noticeable in early fall, often clinging to clothing and pet fur. Vines begin to yellow and die back with first frosts.
seasonality.winter: Annual vine dies completely, leaving only dried stems and scattered seeds. Look for the persistent spiky burs caught in fence wire or dried vegetation.

funFact: This native vine is like nature's velcro inventor - those spiky little burs inspired part of the design for modern hook-and-loop fasteners, and they're so effective at hitchhiking that a single plant can spread its seeds across an entire neighborhood just by grabbing onto passing dogs, hikers, and gardeners!
confusionNotes: The palmately lobed leaves might remind you of a small maple or wild grape, but the climbing habit with tendrils and those unmistakable spiky bur fruits in clusters are dead giveaways. Memory trick: 'Spiky clusters = bur cucumber, smooth grapes = grape vine.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cucumber,' this plant is only distantly related to garden cucumbers and is not edible. It's actually a beneficial native plant that provides food for wildlife and helps prevent soil erosion along waterways, though gardeners sometimes consider it a nuisance when it covers their prized plants.
compareHints: Oneseed bur cucumber is the only member of its genus in New England, making it unique in that regard. Compared to other gourd family members like wild cucumber (Echinocystis), it has much smaller, spikier fruits that form in tight clusters rather than large, papery pods. The single seed per fruit also distinguishes it from most other cucurbit relatives which typically have multiple seeds.
